slides.say: A, B and C represent digits. Given: A A A minus forty-six is equal to B C. B plus C is equal to what?
This is a subtraction puzzle, and the choices also use letters as digits. [short pause] We'll solve it by reading the same equality as an addition.

[short pause] First write it vertically. A A A minus forty-six is B C. Add forty-six to both sides, and we get B C plus forty-six is A A A. The numbers have not changed. We just have an addition to check now.

Why is addition easier to read? Take A A minus B B equals B B. We can write it as B B plus B B equals A A. Now we can see that B could be one, two, three or four. Five is too large: fifty-five plus fifty-five is a hundred ten, which has three digits, not two.

Back to our question: B C plus forty-six is A A A. We add two two-digit numbers and get a three-digit result, so the hundreds digit must be one. That digit is A. So A is one, and A A A is a hundred eleven.
at: so the hundreds digit must be one

slides.say: Now we know the whole three-digit number. We could continue column by column: C plus six ends in one, so C is five and we carry one. But we can find the whole result directly by subtracting. A hundred eleven minus forty-six is sixty-five. So B is six, C is five, and their sum is eleven.
at: C plus six ends in one
so C is five and we carry one

slides.say: We need the choice that represents eleven. A is one, so the two-digit number A A is eleven. Choice number three is our answer. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
at: Choice number three is our answer
